text: Last time, Tiny said eight to three plus four. Wrong. Reward, zero.
And nothing moved. The mistake taught it nothing.
Now watch the same mistake, with one small change.
Eight shrinks! And seven grows!
Now a mistake teaches something. And the change is an idea you already know from school.
Learning from mistakes. Episode two.
Picture two students. Both get forty percent on a test.
One of them usually scores twenty-five percent.
Then forty is brilliant! Party time.
The other one usually scores ninety.
Uh oh. Then forty is a disaster.
Same score. Opposite news. What matters is the score, compared with the usual score.
That’s the whole idea. Instead of the raw reward, we use the reward, minus the usual reward.
In papers, the usual reward is called the baseline, and the difference is called the advantage.
For Tiny right now, the usual reward is about twenty-two percent, because that’s how often it says seven.
So when it says eight, the advantage is zero minus point two two. Negative. So eight gets pushed down.
And when it says seven?
One minus point two two. Plus point seven eight. Seven goes up. Now every answer teaches something.
Second knob: how big a nudge. Think of a shower tap.
Turn it a hair, and you’re waiting forever for warm water.
Crank it, and you’re scalded.
Same with Tiny. Start every answer at twenty-five percent, reward seven just once, and change the step size.
Step a half: seven goes to thirty-five percent. Step two: seventy-one. Step ten: basically a hundred, from one lucky answer.
Total certainty from one try? That’s reckless.
In papers, this knob is the learning rate. Too small is slow. Too big jumps to conclusions.
Third: you can’t reward what you never try.
Like ordering the same dish at the same restaurant, every single time.
Exactly. You’d never find out the special is better. If Tiny gives seven almost no chance, it almost never says it, and never sees it rewarded.
So we keep some randomness, and sample several answers to each question. More tries, more chances to stumble on something good.
Now, a test of the baseline. Give every answer ten bonus points, just for showing up.
Seven still beats eight by exactly the same amount. With no baseline, what happens to learning?
Pause, and have a guess.
A. Nothing changes. Seven’s still the best answer, so it still wins.
That’s the trap. It’s C. Learning falls apart.
These are real results from the lab code. Twenty runs each, sixty steps.
Honest scores, no baseline: seven reaches ninety-seven percent.
Add ten points for everyone: twenty-three percent. Lower than where it started! And the runs disagree wildly.
But why?!
Every answer that comes up gets a big positive score, so every answer gets pushed up. Whatever happens to come up early snowballs.
Subtract the usual score, and the ten points cancel out. Ninety-six percent. The baseline buys reliability.
And here’s the whole thing in numpy. A few lines.
Roll Tiny’s die eight times.
Look up each score, and subtract the batch’s average. That’s the baseline.
Nudge each answer by its advantage.
And take a step, sized by the learning rate.
Wait, that’s it? That’s the algorithm?
That’s it. Twenty-five percent to ninety-six, in sixty steps. In papers, it’s called REINFORCE.
Quick recap.
Compare each reward with the usual reward, and mistakes start teaching.
Pick the step size carefully. Too small is slow, and too big is reckless.
And keep exploring, because you can’t reward what you never try.
Okay, but here’s what bugs me.
Tiny only ever gets one question. A real model gets thousands. Some easy, some brutal.
Right. On an easy one, the usual score might be high. On a hard one, really low.
So one average for everything isn’t fair. Usual... compared to what?
Compare each answer with other answers to the same question. A group. Next episode: groups and advantages, the heart of GRPO.
Run the REINFORCE lab, and try the plus ten experiment yourself.
See you in the next episode!
